uncovered_requirements.text: User can mine file co-occurrence from git history, counting how often file pairs appear in the same commit
User can compute temporal coupling scores with configurable thresholds (min_shared_commits, min_coupling_degree) to identify implicitly related files
User can filter out mass-refactoring commits by inverse file-count weighting, so commits touching 50+ files contribute less coupling signal than focused changes
User can have co-change pairs injected into the debug context bundle, so `/nf:debug` surfaces implicit coupling when investigating bugs in related files
User can compute per-file churn scores from git log with streaming parsing that handles repos with 10K+ commits without exceeding maxBuffer
User can compute per-file cyclomatic complexity by counting decision points in the tree-sitter AST, producing a language-agnostic complexity score
User can compute a hotspot risk score as the normalized intersection of churn and complexity, identifying files that are both frequently changed and structurally complex
User can exclude high-noise paths (generated files, vendored dirs, mass-refactor commits) and normalize by file size to reduce false positive hotspot signals
User can have high-risk hotspot files automatically escalate quorum fan-out in `nf-prompt.js`, so agents receive more review capacity on risky code changes
User can deliver file contents to LLMs in XML-style tagged format (`<file path="...">...</file>`) that preserves structure while reducing token overhead vs raw source inclusion
User can escape XML-special characters in packed content via an `escapeXml()` helper that handles `<`, `>`, `&`, `"`, `'` — preventing malformed XML output
User can invoke `context-packer.cjs` as a single entry point that orchestrates all Repowise intelligence modules (skeleton, hotspot, co-change) and produces a unified packed context output
User can compress skeleton detail level based on a token budget, so that the system adapts output to fit within context window constraints rather than producing uniformly detailed output
User can parse source files into ASTs via `web-tree-sitter` WASM with lazy initialization (Parser.init() on first use, not at CLI startup)
User can extract a structural skeleton from parsed AST showing function/class/method names with line ranges (start-end), producing ~5-10% of original token count
User can parse JavaScript, TypeScript, and Python files out of the box via bundled grammar packages; additional languages available via optional grammar installation
User can see hotspot risk scores and coupling degree embedded in skeleton output, so skeleton entries for high-risk or highly-coupled code are annotated with behavioral intelligence
